crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: The threshold of machine authorship is the line between human creative or inventive contribution and output generated by a machine.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries sit at the meeting point of agency law, fiduciary duty, corporate governance, and AI regulation.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: Liability when agents interact covers the legal questions that arise when two or more autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents exchange instructions, negotiate, transact, or act on shared systems and a loss, breach, or injury follows.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes and evidentiary standards concerns how courts, tribunals, arbitrators, and regulators decide whether a synthetic or manipulated audio, image, or video can be admitted, authenticated, and weighed as evidence.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation is a legal and policy claim that a person affected by an automated decision can obtain meaningful information about how that decision was reached.

sections.body: Emerging Legal Frameworks is the part of AI law that asks who or what is responsible when AI systems create, decide, or cause harm. In practice, courts and regulators are handling disputes over machine authorship, autonomous entities, multi-agent liability, deepfake evidence, and the right to an explanation. The site currently tracks 149 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows how quickly these questions have moved from speculation to docket. The work is not about building a single new body of law from scratch. It is about applying existing doctrines, such as agency, negligence, evidence, and due process, to systems that act in ways their operators may not fully predict.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some questions have partial answers. Copyright offices and courts have begun to say that human authorship is required for protection, but the line between assistance and authorship remains contested. Liability when agents interact is harder, because harm can emerge from many small automated decisions rather than one clear act. Deepfake evidence has forced courts to revisit authentication, and the right to an explanation is still uneven, with some regimes requiring reasons and others offering only summaries. The site tracks 29 AI case law precedents and 7066 state AI bills, which together show a field with many proposals and few settled rules.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section follow a sequence from creation to accountability. The Threshold of Machine Authorship sets out the baseline question of whether a machine can be an author or inventor. Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries then examines whether an AI system or its manager can hold duties, and Liability When Agents Interact extends that to harms produced by multiple systems. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards turns to proof, asking how courts should treat synthetic media offered as evidence. The Right to an Explanation closes the set by looking at what a person is owed when an automated decision goes against them. A reader would go to the first page for authorship, the middle pages for entity and multi-agent responsibility, and the final pages for evidence and explanation.
